name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
title: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
answer: Fabricated citations are references that look plausible but point to papers, authors, journals or DOIs that do not exist, or that misattribute real work to the wrong source. The problem sits inside research integrity and scholarly governance, and it now overlaps with AI writing tools that can generate a reference list faster than any human can check it. Scope covers detection, correction, retraction and the editorial rules that decide who is accountable when a false reference reaches print. It also covers the quieter case of a real paper cited for a claim it never made.

sections.body: Fabricated citations are references that look plausible but point to papers, authors, journals or DOIs that do not exist, or that misattribute real work to the wrong source. The problem sits inside research integrity and scholarly governance, and it now overlaps with AI writing tools that can generate a reference list faster than any human can check it. Scope covers detection, correction, retraction and the editorial rules that decide who is accountable when a false reference reaches print. It also covers the quieter case of a real paper cited for a claim it never made.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Checking a citation runs on a small stack: a DOI resolver, a publisher landing page, a bibliographic database, and the paper itself. Reference managers such as Zotero or EndNote store the record, while Crossref and Retraction Watch supply the status signals that a formatted reference alone will not show.A citation that cannot be resolved to a real record fails at the first step, before any judgement about its content is needed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is mostly verification by hand, done in a fixed order: resolve the identifier, confirm the title, authors, venue and year, then open the paper and check that the cited claim appears in it. Automated screening helps at scale by flagging references that do not resolve, that share suspicious patterns, or that cluster around a single implausible source, but a person still reads the passage. Reviewers and editors are the usual checkpoint, and some journals now ask authors to supply the source for each factual statement. Where a claim is contested, the useful move is to trace it back to the primary study rather than to a review that repeats it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Responsibility is split between authors, reviewers, editors and institutions, and most guidelines treat fabricated references as misconduct rather than as a formatting error. Publishers can correct or retract, and a retraction notice is itself a citable record that later readers need to find. Provenance matters because a reference is a claim about where knowledge came from, so a false one corrupts the trail even when the surrounding text is sound. Disclosure of AI assistance in drafting is increasingly required, and it does not transfer responsibility away from the named author. Nothing here is legal advice, and specific cases turn on the policies of the journal and the institution involved.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Detection is shifting from spot checks to routine screening at submission, with identifier validation and consistency checks built into editorial systems. The harder problem is semantic: a reference can resolve perfectly and still misrepresent what the cited paper found, and that is not caught by any resolver. Expect more emphasis on claim level provenance, where each statement carries a link to the exact passage that supports it, and more pressure on publishers to publish the checks they run. Tools will keep improving at finding false references, which pushes the residual risk toward subtle misattribution in otherwise clean bibliographies.
